Every row of an infinite table can approach the same number while a diagonal through the table stays at a different number forever.

Consider the rational numbers

The first row eventually becomes zero. So does the second, and so does every later row. Each row represents the same limiting number. Yet the diagonal entries satisfy for every . Advancing through both indices at once has preserved the initial error in each new row.

In this table, moving one place farther along each row repairs the failure. The entries are all zero. What matters is knowing how far along a row to go before using its value in the next calculation.

The familiar construction of the real numbers contains a precise account of this problem. It explains how a hierarchy of approximations can return one answer, how a finite proof can control an unbounded family of requests, and why possessing a convergent description can leave the practical answer out of reach. The decisive information is a proved relation connecting what a finite calculation can obtain to the conclusion we seek about the infinite construction. Finding such a relation, and making it economical to use, can be the main mathematical achievement.

Choosing how far to look

A rational Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose terms eventually become arbitrarily close to one another. Two such sequences represent the same real number when their difference tends to zero. This identification lets many different approximations stand for one point.

Now suppose is itself a Cauchy sequence of real numbers. For each , present by a rational Cauchy row

There are two independent demands. Terms within a row must settle toward the real represented by that row. The reals represented by later rows must settle toward one another. The opening table shows why a common index supplies insufficient control over those demands.

Choose far enough along row that

and set . Regarding a rational as the real represented by its constant sequence, we obtain

For two selected entries, the triangle inequality gives

Given a positive tolerance, take both indices large enough that each of the three terms is less than one third of it. The outer Cauchy hypothesis supplies control of the middle term. Our choices within the rows supply control of the other two. Thus is a rational Cauchy sequence.

Let be the real represented by that sequence. The embedded rationals converge to their own class , a direct consequence of the definition of the Cauchy construction. Therefore

The sequence of reals has a limit among the reals. We have established completeness by returning a two-level description to a single rational sequence.

The schedule is the essential connective information. It makes the accuracy obtained inside a row answer to the accuracy required when that row joins the outer calculation. Different schedules can work, and their outputs represent the same limiting real. The point remains independent of the particular presentation used to reach it.

This is also why completing a metric space a second time adds no further points once its first completion is complete, in the classical setting and up to canonical isometry. A Cauchy sequence in an already complete space has a unique limit there. Sending its equivalence class to that limit preserves distances and inverts the constant-sequence embedding. In the rational case, the estimate above displays the absorption explicitly.

Calling the result a point lets later arguments use this coordinated construction as one object. We can add it to another real, compare distances, or apply a continuous function because those operations respect the identification of equivalent approximations. The simple notation rests on relations among the finite stages. A chosen representative exposes the rational data again, and quantitative estimates determine how accurately we must obtain them. The completed point summarizes this organization. Establishing and using the underlying relations is the substantive mathematical work here.

A useful way to expose the role of quantitative control is to compare consecutive approximations. Suppose , where is a proved error allowance for that step. Repeated application of the triangle inequality gives, for ,

If the remaining allowances have a summable tail

then every later approximation lies within of . Completeness supplies a limit , with . For , the geometric-series identity gives . A rule governing individual steps and an estimate of their remaining total control an arbitrarily long continuation of the calculation.

The distinction between local information and global control is explicit here. A bound on each step becomes useful for convergence through a bound on how the steps accumulate. Merely knowing that the steps tend to zero allows the harmonic partial sums, whose steps are and whose values diverge. Even summability can leave the effective tail bound inaccessible, as the computable example below will show.

Summable step bounds give one sufficient presentation. A Cauchy sequence can also approach its limit with infinite total variation, as does for . Its convergence is established by a different estimate. The useful organization depends on the sequence. What matters is finding a relation that makes the passage from a finite observation to an unbounded family of later observations something we can justify.

What a finite description promises

The proof chose sufficiently late entries. An executable version must obtain them when asked.

Suppose a single procedure returns a rational satisfying

The word single matters. Given the row number and precision, the procedure must reach the corresponding approximation. Separate assertions that every row has some algorithm leave this uniform access to be established.

Suppose we also have an outer Cauchy modulus , meaning

Passing to the limit in the second index shows that . Hence the explicit request

returns a rational with

Half the error allowance goes to the outer approximation and half to evaluating it. If and are computable, so is this procedure.

In computable analysis, a rapidly converging rational sequence of this kind is a standard way to give access to a real. The request is a precision, and the response is an approximation with a specified error bound. Brattka's tutorial develops the representation and the importance of uniform access when passing from individual numbers to sequences and functions. 1

A finite program can answer indefinitely many such requests, completing each in finite time. A finite proof can establish its error bound for every requested precision. Those two finite objects have different jobs. The program produces values. The proof justifies the relationship between every produced value and the real it represents.

Zeilberger makes this computational demand explicit in Opinion 146. His account of the decimal truncations asks for an algorithm that takes a symbolic positive rational tolerance and returns a threshold , beyond which the truncations stay within of one. He interprets the assertion entirely through finite symbols. In the classical account used here, that procedure also supplies an effective rate of convergence. The computational content gives the two interpretations substantial common ground. 16

The equivalence relation defining the real deliberately ignores the speed of a name. Two sequences with very different rates can represent the same point. This makes the point independent of how we first approached it. Calculating with that point requires access through some particular presentation, whose speed and available error bounds affect what we can afford to do. Mathematical equality leaves these operational differences intact.

Classical real numbers have a wider scope. There are only countably many finite programs and uncountably many reals. A general Cauchy name can therefore contain information that no finite program generates. A procedure may also receive a name as input, querying its approximations without possessing a program that created it. Representing an arbitrary real and computing a particular real are separate mathematical questions.

Foundational assumptions also affect the available data. Selecting representatives for all rows can invoke countable choice. Classically, canonical rational approximations give a completeness proof without it. Constructive settings make the availability of representatives and moduli consequential, as Lubarsky's countermodels show. The explicit procedure above states its required names and modulus at the input. 2

A computable sequence with an inaccessible rate

The missing modulus can carry decisive information.

Number computer programs by the nonnegative integers. At stage , run each of the first programs for steps, with its own index as input. Let be the indices observed to halt, and form

Each stage involves a finite computation and returns an exact rational. The sequence is nondecreasing and bounded by , so it converges to a real .

An effective procedure for approximating to every requested accuracy would decide which programs eventually halt. To see why, suppose the halting status of indices below has already been recovered and subtract their contributions from . Put . If program halts, the remainder is at least . If it never halts, the remainder is at most

Approximating that remainder to error less than distinguishes the two cases. Beginning at and proceeding inductively would decide the halting problem. Thus is noncomputable. A computable Cauchy modulus for would compute , so such a modulus is unavailable.

Its computable increments are nonnegative and summable. An effective bound tending to zero for their tails would compute , so such a bound is unavailable. Even when every individual step can be calculated, the information needed to control its accumulation can remain inaccessible.

This is a version of the phenomenon associated with Specker sequences, computable nondecreasing bounded rational sequences with noncomputable limits. Powell discusses their effect on extracting quantitative information from convergence theorems. 3

The obstruction resides in the future contributions. A long quiet stretch cannot certify that a particular program will never halt later. Every term is accessible, and the sequence has a perfectly definite classical limit. The demand for a justified stopping point introduces information absent from the rule producing its terms.

There is, however, a revealing finite question that this sequence can answer. Supply a positive rational accuracy and a computable rule prescribing how far ahead to inspect from any starting point . Ask for a window

throughout which all the values stay within of one another.

For any computable nondecreasing rational sequence in , there is a finite search. Start at , and set . A failed window has

More than successive failures would consume more than the total available increase of one. Testing endpoints therefore finds a successful window among the first candidates. Monotonicity controls every intermediate value. The indices requested by may be enormous, so the number of tests alone leaves their execution cost open.

The guarantee covers the requested window. A later change can occur beyond it. The corresponding classical formulation quantifies over every horizon function, including noncomputable ones,

This property is called metastability and is classically equivalent to Cauchy convergence. Its computational requests differ from obtaining one starting point that controls the entire infinite tail. For computable and rational , the finite search just given supplies an executable response. This change in the form of the question can expose finite information that a global convergence rate conceals. 3 4

The classical equivalence makes the role of the horizon precise. A Cauchy sequence satisfies every requested window once its whole tail is sufficiently close. If the sequence fails to be Cauchy, some fixed positive tolerance has a violating pair beyond every starting point. Define to extend to one such pair, selecting the first in a fixed enumeration. Every requested window then fails. The quantification over all detects exactly this possibility, even when the detecting horizon cannot be computed.

Infinity enters here through the range and order of the requests we must answer. The same sequence supports a finite search for every supplied observation window while withholding an effective guarantee about its whole future. The logical form of a theorem affects what a calculation can obtain from it.

Extracting such information from proofs is an established research programme. Proof mining investigates the effective bounds, algorithms, and dependence on parameters that can be recovered from qualitative arguments. Kohlenbach's survey develops this approach in nonlinear analysis. The form of the conclusion and the available quantitative hypotheses govern what can be extracted. 17

How accuracy passes through a function

Completion gives a point to a Cauchy description. Continuity governs what happens when another operation acts on that description.

This can even define an operation on the completed space. Let be dense in a metric space , and let be uniformly continuous, with complete. Given converging to , uniform continuity makes Cauchy, so it has a limit in . Interleaving two sequences approaching the same shows that both yield the same limit. Defining therefore gives a well-defined extension, and the same uniform control proves its continuity. The operation respects the identification that created the point. 15

The hypothesis matters. The function is continuous on the positive rationals, but its values diverge along , approaching the missing endpoint zero. Uniform continuity is a sufficient condition that prevents this failure when extending to the closure.

For a function already defined at , continuity there gives . A quantitative version asks how close the input must be to make the output sufficiently close. Suppose a modulus satisfies, on the relevant domain,

Assume that, from the supplied name of , we can obtain rational approximations in the domain with any requested error. To approximate within , obtain a rational in the domain within of , then evaluate within . Again, two controlled errors add to the requested tolerance.

The modulus translates output accuracy into input accuracy. An evaluation procedure must then deliver the second bound. Ordinary continuity asserts the existence of suitable local control. A computable implementation requires effective access to enough control and evaluation information. These requirements belong to the representation of the function as well as the representation of its argument. 1

A Lipschitz bound gives a particularly simple translation. If , an input error of at most , for , and an evaluation error of at most suffice. The arithmetic cost of obtaining either accuracy remains a further question.

Even an elementary continuous function can demand much more accurate input than its output. For nonnegative ,

At zero this estimate is attained. If the available information is only , then can range over . Making that range at most wide requires .

After successive square roots, the function is

The same input enclosure allows an output range of width . To limit that range to , require

In this enclosure model near zero, the required number of input bits doubles with every added square root. A compact formula for the composition preserves that dependence. If the input is known symbolically to equal zero, the additional information settles the evaluation immediately. The cost belongs to the function together with the way its input is available.

Thus a hierarchy can collapse to one expression while retaining an expensive demand for precision. Evaluation is already sensitive to how information arrives. Asking a function to reveal one of its roots introduces a further difficulty.

What it takes to find a zero

The intermediate value theorem brings these ideas together. Let be continuous on , with . Classical bisection either encounters a zero or produces nested brackets of length

whose endpoint values retain opposite signs. Nestedness makes both endpoint sequences Cauchy. Completeness supplies their limits, and the vanishing lengths make those limits equal to a point . Continuity then gives

so .

Each ingredient has done a particular job. The bracket rule preserves opposite signs at the endpoints. The length estimate controls location. Completeness produces the point, and continuity connects the endpoint signs to its value. If the endpoints themselves arrive through rational names, their evaluation can be scheduled by the earlier diagonal construction.

For an algorithm receiving a general computable continuous function, exact sign decisions introduce a difficulty. Increasing the accuracy of an evaluation can eventually certify a strictly positive or strictly negative value. An exact zero may keep every enclosing interval touching both signs. The classical branch that asks whether the midpoint value equals zero has no general terminating test.

The difficulty also has a geometric form. Define on

Set .

For , every has opposite signs at its endpoints and is 1-Lipschitz. For , its unique root is . For , its unique root is . At , every point of is a root.

As approaches zero from its two sides, the forced choices of root approach different points. Arbitrarily close input functions therefore demand separated answers from any rule selecting one root. The continuity of evaluation and the continuity of solution selection are distinct properties.

Computable analysis states the consequence precisely. In the standard representation of continuous functions on , there is no uniform algorithm selecting an exact root from every computable continuous function with a strict endpoint sign change. Each individual such function nevertheless has some computable root. Restricting the input to functions with a unique zero restores a uniform computable operation, with computational cost still depending on the input. 5

For the unique-zero case on , divide the current rational bracket into thirds. Evaluate the function at both interior division points in parallel, refining until one value has a certified nonzero sign. Uniqueness guarantees that both points cannot be zeros, so this search terminates. Keep the interval joining that point to the endpoint of opposite sign. Its length is at most two thirds of the previous length. Repetition yields a computable name for the root while allowing each successful sign test to take as much precision as it needs.

Individual computable roots exist in the general case for another reason. If the zero set contains a nondegenerate interval, it contains a rational root. Otherwise every open subinterval contains a rational point with nonzero value, by continuity. A parallel search through rational points in the middle third then supplies a nonzero sign and the same shrinking-bracket construction. These two cases establish existence, while choosing the appropriate case uniformly remains part of the obstruction.

An approximate answer must specify what is small. A small value of is a residual guarantee. A short bracket known to contain a zero gives a location guarantee. For with , the residual at zero is , while the distance to its root is always . A known inverse estimate

converts residual into location error through .

A uniformly computable nested sequence of rational root-containing brackets, with widths tending to zero, already supplies a name for an exact root. To answer a precision request, search until the rational width is sufficiently small. Consequently, producing compatible brackets at all accuracies carries the solution-selection obligation with it.

Zeilberger's Opinion 160 asks for a different output, an atomic sign-changing interval at a fixed symbolic mesh . His earlier account of discrete analysis treats as formal degeneration. That fixed-mesh conclusion has a direct finite interpretation. Recovering the classical exact-root conclusion calls for a further argument connecting scales, establishing a point, and relating it to the original function. 6 7

These distinctions let mathematical purposes remain explicit. A finite location tolerance may completely meet one application. Another calculation may require a value that can be refined whenever a later operation demands it. A symbolic certificate may establish a property for every precision at once. The question being asked determines which relationship has to be proved.

A continuum problem inside finite systems

Numerical analysis encounters the same structure when it replaces a differential equation by a family of finite problems. Mesh refinement supplies one index. Solving the resulting algebraic system supplies another. Their interaction can be calculated exactly in a simple example.

Consider

The exact solution is . Measure an error , with square-integrable weak derivative and zero endpoint values, by its energy norm

Divide the interval into equal cells of length . Let consist of continuous functions that are linear on each cell and vanish at the endpoints. The Galerkin solution satisfies

In this example, is the nodal interpolant of . Indeed, the interpolation error vanishes at the ends of every cell, while is constant there. Its product with the derivative of that error therefore integrates to zero. The interpolant satisfies the displayed Galerkin equations.

On the cell ,

Its squared integral is . Summing over the cells gives the exact discretization error

Now let be the result after iterations of an algebraic solver. Galerkin orthogonality makes the discretization error orthogonal to every function in , including . Expanding the squared norm gives

The two indices from the rational table have returned as two sources of error. Refinement controls the first term. Solver progress controls the second. An exact solve on a fixed mesh leaves the error . Refining the mesh while maintaining insufficient algebraic accuracy can also leave a persistent error. Choose so that

Then

This is a controlled diagonal through the family of numerical calculations. It includes a rate, and it states which norm measures success. The exact equalities are specific to this example. The underlying projection argument is standard Galerkin theory, developed in Schöberl's account of coercive variational problems. 8

For a general bounded coercive bilinear form on a real Hilbert space , assume

With a bounded load and a closed conforming Galerkin subspace , Céa's estimate gives

Convergence requires the best-approximation error on the right to vanish. A rate needs corresponding approximation and regularity estimates. Parameter-dependent problems also require attention to the constants. Each computation can use a finite space, while the theorem connects its answer to the infinite-dimensional target and controls what happens as the spaces change. 8

Making the error affordable to measure

The stopping rule above uses an error relative to , which is precisely the solution still being computed. We must obtain a usable bound without making its evaluation as expensive as finishing the original problem.

In the interior nodal basis of our example, the exact system is

This matrix is the Laplacian of a weighted path with its endpoint values fixed. Extend an interior vector by , and let record neighboring differences, . Direct multiplication gives

Each edge contributes a neighboring difference to the energy. Refining the mesh repeats the rule on a longer path, while the approximation theorem connects the resulting family to the continuum equation. The energy of a vector sums contributions across the whole path, and its small-energy modes can extend across many edges. The spectral estimates below control the resulting global response.

For an approximate coefficient vector , put . Take on every mesh. Then and , giving

Yet on every mesh. A fixed positive absolute tolerance on this residual eventually accepts an approximation that has made no progress. The Euclidean norm here measures the vector of residuals against the nodal test functions. Both those functions and their number change with the mesh. The relative residual stays equal to one. Interpreting the absolute residual requires a relation to the mesh and the intended error norm.

For a general approximation , the coefficient error is , so

As with the root-location estimate, the inverse response connects the residual to the error in the chosen norm. This relation also survives a change of basis. If old coefficients equal times new coefficients, with invertible, the same approximation has transformed matrix and residual . Direct substitution gives

Rescaling the basis can make the raw residual norm arbitrarily small while leaving the represented function unchanged. The inverse operator compensates for that coordinate change, preserving the algebraic energy error inside . A zero matrix residual means that the equations hold for every test function in that space. The mesh estimate accounts for the continuum error that remains. Computing the inverse action may itself require a substantial solve.

Suppose instead that a symmetric positive-definite matrix admits a cheaper inverse action, with proved bounds

Here means for every vector . Reversing the order under inversion gives

Thus

For a target , one sufficient allocation is

Half the squared-error allowance goes to discretization and half to the algebraic solve. Other allocations can be more economical. Their validity and cost can be investigated because the error identity makes their consequences explicit.

Uniform control adds another requirement. If and remain fixed throughout a mesh family, they bound the condition number of the symmetric transformed operator by . This is the spectral comparison used in positive-definite preconditioning. Its computational value also depends on constructing and applying its inverse economically. 9

Finite solvability alone leaves substantial room for deterioration across a family. Apply the tridiagonal matrix to the vectors with entries , for . The sine addition formula gives

so

Every matrix is finite and positive definite. Its condition number nevertheless grows without bound as the mesh is refined. The family presents a mathematical problem that no inventory of the properties of one fixed matrix resolves. The present tridiagonal system still admits a direct solve in arithmetic operations, using bounded work per row in elimination and back substitution. Conditioning and the work required by a particular solution method are separate questions. 9

This example also admits a certificate using only the residual norm. Concavity places sine above its endpoint chord on , giving for . The smallest eigenvalue therefore satisfies , and

The stopping rule makes the algebraic error at most , as requested earlier. A finite residual calculation now certifies the chosen balance. Its threshold changes with the mesh, making the relationship between the two levels explicit.

The displayed error identities use exact matrices and residuals. They apply to any represented coefficient vector, including one produced by floating-point arithmetic. Certifying their numerical evaluation requires bounds on rounding errors. More general discretizations can also introduce quadrature, geometric, and coefficient errors that must enter the final estimate. Ball arithmetic, as developed in Arb, supplies enclosures through finite computations, while truncation and approximation bounds still require the mathematics appropriate to the problem. 10

The one-dimensional example makes all these relations visible because its solution is explicit. In a difficult problem, obtaining the analogue of its error identity, a sharp bound, or a cheap inverse action can be the research contribution.

Finite proofs of infinite obligations

Exact cancellation supplies another way for a finite relation to control an unbounded family. Wilf and Zeilberger's theory of summation certificates begins with functions satisfying

Here is a nonnegative integer and is an integer. Summing over a finite interval leaves only its boundary terms,

Suppose each fixed- row of and has finite support. Choose the endpoints beyond the relevant supports. The boundary terms vanish, so satisfies . Its initial value determines the sum for every . For infinite support, absolute summability of the -rows and as suffice for this same conclusion. The hypotheses give the local identity its global force. 18

In the hypergeometric setting, a rational function can encode relative to , making the displayed relation reducible to a polynomial identity after denominators are cleared, wherever the ratios are defined. Exceptional indices and boundary behaviour still require justification. The certificate controls a whole family because its algebra and those conditions work together. The earlier summable-step estimate controlled accumulation by bounding it. Here the relation arranges exact cancellation.

A finite certificate can also control a tail whose terms remain present. Analytic estimates make this possible even when a computation never stores those terms.

Gameiro and Lessard's rigorous computation of PDE equilibria uses a finite collection of Fourier coefficients together with analytic bounds for the remaining coefficients. Their construction combines finitely many inequalities for the retained part with a tail estimate covering infinitely many indices. When the bounds establish that an associated map sends a ball into itself and contracts there, the contraction theorem supplies a unique equilibrium within that ball. 11

The finite verification has force because the analytic estimate quantifies over the omitted tail. A large computed prefix would leave that obligation unresolved on its own. The proof determines why the uncomputed coordinates are controlled and how the resulting infinite sequence solves the original equation.

A specific relation supplies the control in each example. The Cauchy estimate combines accuracy within a row with convergence across rows. The WZ identity converts a change in the sum into boundary terms whose vanishing must be justified. In the Poisson problem, Galerkin orthogonality separates mesh error from solver error, and a spectral bound converts a residual into a solution-error estimate. The Fourier tail bound covers all omitted coefficients. Each relation specifies what the finite work establishes and which hypotheses support its reach beyond the terms explicitly examined.

Finding the relation that supports such a justification can be the difficult part of the mathematics. A sharper tail estimate can make a previously inconclusive computation decisive. A less expensive certificate can make verification affordable. Once established, such a relation becomes equipment for later calculations, carrying its hypotheses and error bounds with it.

The numerical research bet

This perspective helps specify the research direction I favor in Abstraction is no refuge from AI. I would concentrate on reliable adaptive sparse computation, where a useful representation must preserve the relevant operator relationships and make accuracy affordable across a declared workload. 12

An explicit finite matrix can contain all the input data while leaving the economical representation undiscovered. A coarse space must approximate sufficiently well the error components that inexpensive relaxation removes slowly. A diagnostic must reveal enough about those components to justify its own expense. A uniform theorem must identify which constants survive refinement, changing coefficients, or another declared variation of the problem.

The examples here suggest a concrete sequence of research questions. What error reaches the requested output? Which observation bounds that error? How accurately must a subordinate calculation be performed? When does obtaining a sharper bound save more work than it costs? An effective schedule answers these questions with enough precision to direct a computation.

Zeilberger's computational philosophy already joins representation to these questions of cost. His Enquiry urges mathematicians to make computational frameworks explicit and teach them to computers, while observing that a short program can take an impractically long time. Theorems for a Price examines the expense of proof certificates and proposes accepting weaker assurance when full verification costs too much. The numerical programme here specifies the required accuracy and assurance through the declared task, then includes the cost of meeting them in the comparison. 19 20

Established numerical methods already automate substantial parts of this process. Inexact Newton methods tie the accuracy of an inner linear solve to progress in the outer nonlinear problem. Eisenstat and Walker study forcing terms satisfying

Their choices aim to avoid oversolving a local model whose prediction may be poor far from the solution. Their convergence statements have local regularity and initial-point hypotheses, while their experiments address the practical expense of the choices. 13

Automatic construction also has a substantial history. Brandt's algebraic coarsening work uses compatible relaxation to assess proposed coarse variables and guide improvements when slowly reduced errors reveal inadequate representation. The decision about what to retain can itself become an algorithm. 14

These methods set a demanding baseline for specialist and AI collaboration. My wager concerns whether specialists can help discover further useful tests, estimates, and constructions more economically than equally equipped autonomous systems, with a larger net contribution on the numerical portfolio than on the structural portfolio chosen for comparison. The comparison must charge for producing and checking guidance, unsuccessful investigations, and the costs of the final method. Successful techniques must then enter the common equipment used on fresh problems. 12

The appeal of this direction is the recurring mathematical work exposed by the examples. A theorem may establish convergence while leaving its rate expensive to obtain. A computable procedure may meet every precision request at an impractical cost. A fast calculation may need a stronger relationship between its residual and the intended answer. Each situation gives research a definite obligation to address, and a way to examine whether the proposed improvement pays.

Those obligations are open to human, machine, and collaborative solutions. The diagonal argument makes the information required of a successful construction explicit.

Returning from infinity

The opening table contains nothing difficult at any individual entry. Its failure arises from how entries are selected across the table. The repaired diagonal succeeds because an accuracy requirement governs that selection.

The question we intend to answer changes which information matters. The Specker sequence admits computable finite windows of stability while withholding a computable rate for its whole tail. A continuous function can be easy to evaluate while selecting one of its roots is unstable. The inverse-energy relation preserves the meaning of algebraic error across coordinate changes, while the mesh estimate controls the continuum error left by an exact finite solve.

This suggests a way to read an infinite construction. Ask what finite question it enables us to answer, which quantified relationship justifies the answer, and what information remains necessary to obtain it. Identifying equivalent approximations gives one real number. What we can do with that number depends on the relations among its approximations. In the constructions examined here, infinity serves as an organizing principle for identities, compatibility conditions, and quantitative bounds across finite stages. The apparent simplicity of a completed infinite object can conceal the intricate finitary work that sustains it. Effective calculation requires access to the particular approximations and error bounds a task demands. A finite proof can range over infinitely many demands because it explains the relationship shared by their answers.

To make a construction elementary is to make that relationship available for further thought. The point, the estimate, and the procedure then become equipment for the next problem. Infinity enters the work as a structure of obligations that mathematics can sometimes organize, transfer, and discharge with remarkable economy.

  13. Stanley C. Eisenstat and Homer F. Walker, Choosing the Forcing Terms in an Inexact Newton Method, SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 17, 16–32, 1996. Relates forcing terms to local convergence and examines their role in avoiding oversolving. Author's paper ↩
  14. Achi Brandt, General Highly Accurate Algebraic Coarsening, Electronic Transactions on Numerical Analysis 10, 1–20, 2000, especially §3. Develops compatible relaxation as a way to assess and improve coarse-variable selection. Paper ↩
  15. Jean-François Babadjian, Didier Smets, and Franck Sueur, Basic Functional Analysis, course notes, October 18, 2011, §1.2.4, Theorem 1.2.3. Establishes extension of a uniformly continuous function from a dense subset to a complete target. Notes ↩
  16. Doron Zeilberger, Opinion 146, September 12, 2015. States the decimal-convergence claim through an algorithm from symbolic rational tolerance to a symbolic threshold, while rejecting quantification over infinite sets. Opinion ↩
  17. Ulrich Kohlenbach, Proof-theoretic Methods in Nonlinear Analysis, 2018 ICM survey, especially §1. Discusses extracting effective bounds, algorithms, parameter dependence, and weaker hypotheses from proofs. The present essay brings established methods into a connected account of approximation, certification, and computational cost. Author manuscript ↩
  18. Herbert S. Wilf and Doron Zeilberger, Rational Functions Certify Combinatorial Identities, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 3, 147–158, 1990, especially §2. The WZ relation, telescoping proof, and boundary hypotheses support the summation argument above. The linked manuscript is dated January 25, 1989. Author manuscript ↩
  19. Doron Zeilberger, An Enquiry Concerning Human (and Computer!) [Mathematical] Understanding, in Cristian S. Calude, ed., Randomness & Complexity, from Leibniz to Chaitin, World Scientific, 383–410, 2007, especially §§1.14–1.18. Develops the relation among computational frameworks, representations, and execution cost. Author manuscript ↩
  20. Doron Zeilberger, Theorems for a Price: Tomorrow's Semi-Rigorous Mathematical Culture, Notices of the American Mathematical Society 40, 978–981, 1993. Discusses the cost of obtaining proof certificates and proposes semi-rigorous alternatives. Author manuscript ↩
